author: Sachin Sharma
content:
A lift panel in a Delhi mall shows a button marked B2 — two floors below the ground. A weather app says Shimla is at −4 degrees. A parent mutters that the account is −500 after a bounced payment. Every one of these is class 6 maths integers in disguise, and that is exactly why the NCERT Integers chapter matters: it hands children a single, tidy number system for the whole world of ‘below zero’, ‘owed’ and ‘lost’. Until now a six-year’s maths stopped at zero. This chapter opens the door on the other side of it.

I have taught this chapter to plenty of eleven-year-olds, and the single biggest hurdle is not the arithmetic — it is the shift in thinking that a number can sit to the left of zero. Get that picture right and the rest follows almost on its own.

What integers actually are

Integers are the whole numbers together with their negatives: … −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 … and so on in both directions. The positive integers are the counting numbers you already know. The negative integers are their mirror images on the far side of zero. Zero itself is an integer, but it is neither positive nor negative — it is the fence-post everything is measured from.

Notice what is not here: no fractions, no decimals. Half a degree or 2.5 rupees are real, but they are not integers. This chapter deals only in whole steps.

Where negatives show up in real life

  • Temperature below zero — a Leh night at −12 degrees Celsius.
  • Depth below sea level — a diver at −30 metres, or Kuttanad’s farmland sitting below the sea.
  • Money owed — a balance of −200 means you owe 200.
  • Floors below ground — a basement parking level marked −1 or −2.
  • Years before a fixed point, scores in a game where you can lose points, and so on.

The integer number line

Draw a horizontal line, mark 0 in the middle, then step off equal spaces. Positives go to the right, negatives to the left, each a mirror of its positive twin. This one picture does most of the heavy lifting in the chapter, so I make students draw their own rather than copy a printed one.

Two rules of the number line settle almost every question:

  • The further right, the greater the value. So 2 is greater than −5, even though 5 ‘feels’ bigger — and −1 is greater than −9.
  • Every number has an opposite the same distance from zero — 6 and −6, 3 and −3. Opposites always add up to 0.

Ordering and comparing integers

Because ‘right means greater’, comparing integers is just reading the line left to right. A cold-day ordering makes it stick: −8 degrees is colder than −3 degrees, which is colder than 0, which is colder than 5. Written as an ordering, −8 < −3 < 0 < 5. The counter-intuitive bit — that −8 is smaller than −3 even though 8 is bigger than 3 — is where most marks are lost, so I labour it.

Adding and subtracting integers

Two ways to think about addition, and I teach both because different children click with different pictures.

On the number line: start at the first number. To add a positive, hop right; to add a negative, hop left. For −3 + 5, start at −3 and hop 5 to the right — you land on 2.

By the rules: same signs, add and keep the sign (−4 + −3 = −7). Different signs, subtract the smaller from the larger and take the sign of the bigger one (−7 + 4 = −3). Subtraction becomes addition of the opposite: 5 − 8 is the same as 5 + (−8) = −3.

SituationAs an integer sumAnswer
Temperature rises 5 from −3−3 + 52
Lose 300, then owe 400 more−300 + (−400)−700
Owe 700, repay 500−700 + 500−200
Fall 8 from 5 metres5 − 8−3

Case study: the lift and the diver

Read the passage, then work the questions — this is the exact style the case-study e-book uses.

Ria parks on level −2 of a mall. She takes the lift up to floor 5 to watch a film, then down to floor 3 for dinner. Meanwhile her brother Aman is scuba diving: he descends to −18 metres, rises 6 metres to see a reef, then descends another 9 metres.

  • How many floors did Ria travel from −2 up to 5? From −2 to 5 is 5 − (−2) = 7 floors.
  • After the film she goes to floor 3. How far down is that? From 5 to 3 is 2 floors down.
  • Where does Aman end up? −18 + 6 + (−9) = −21 metres.
  • Who is further from ground level, Ria at −2 or Aman at −21? Aman — his distance from zero is 21, against Ria’s 2.

Case study: the cricket-club account

A colony cricket club starts the month at ₹0. It spends ₹600 on a new bat (−600), collects ₹450 in member fees, then pays ₹200 for ground repair. The balance is −600 + 450 + (−350…) — work it step by step: −600 + 450 = −150, then −150 − 200 = −350. The club is ₹350 in debt, written as −350. Little stories like this turn a cold rule into something a child can picture, which is the whole point of a case study.

The short quiz below covers everything above — ordering, the number line, and adding and subtracting integers. Let your child attempt all eight, then read the explanations together for any misses. quiz.title: Class 6 Integers Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on positive and negative numbers, the number line, ordering, and adding and subtracting integers. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT an integer?
questions.explanation: Integers are whole numbers and their negatives. 2.5 is a decimal, so it is not an integer.
On the number line the value furthest to the right is greatest. −1 is closest to zero, so it is the largest of these.
The opposite is the same distance from zero on the other side. The opposite of −6 is 6, and −6 + 6 = 0.

questions.q: The temperature is −3 degrees and rises by 5 degrees. What is it now?
questions.explanation: Start at −3 and hop 5 to the right on the number line: −3 + 5 = 2.
Same signs: add the numbers and keep the sign. 4 + 3 = 7, so the answer is −7.

questions.q: Order these from smallest to largest: 0, −8, 3, −2
questions.explanation: Reading the number line left to right: −8 is smallest, then −2, then 0, then 3.

questions.q: A diver at −12 metres descends another 7 metres. What is her new depth?

faq.q: What is an integer in Class 6 maths?
faq.a: An integer is any whole number together with its negative: … −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 … Zero is an integer too, but it is neither positive nor negative. Fractions and decimals like 2.5 are not integers.

On the number line, values grow as you move right. Both are left of zero, but −8 sits further left than −3, so −8 is the smaller number. A colder temperature is a handy way to picture it: −8 degrees is colder than −3 degrees.

faq.q: How do you add two integers with different signs?
faq.a: Subtract the smaller number from the larger, then take the sign of the number that was bigger. For −7 + 4, subtract 4 from 7 to get 3, and keep the minus sign because 7 was bigger, giving −3.

faq.q: How is subtraction of integers done?
faq.a: Turn it into addition of the opposite. So 5 − 8 becomes 5 + (−8) = −3, and 4 − (−3) becomes 4 + 3 = 7. Adding the opposite works every time.
